content: 1. If a mother has active pulmonary tuberculosis (TB) and has been treated for less than two months before delivery or if TB is diagnosed after delivery, it is safe for her to breastfeed her infant. Reassure the mother about this. 2. Do not administer the Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccine to the infant at birth. 3. Provide prophylactic isoniazid at a dose of 10 mg/kg orally once daily to the infant. 4. Reassess the infant at six weeks of age, monitoring weight gain and, if possible, performing a chest X-ray. 5. If there are any findings suggestive of active TB disease, initiate a full anti-TB treatment regimen in accordance with national guidelines. 6. If the infant is clinically well and diagnostic tests are negative, continue prophylactic isoniazid to complete a six-month course of treatment. 7. Delay the administration of the BCG vaccine until two weeks after the completion of isoniazid treatment. If the BCG vaccine has already been given, repeat the vaccination two weeks after the end of isoniazid treatment. 8. For neonates and low-birth-weight infants, ensure accurate dosing of medications. For example, phenobarbital should be administered as a loading dose of 20 mg/kg intramuscularly (IM) or intravenously (IV), followed by a maintenance dose of 5 mg/kg per day orally. 9. For infants with respiratory symptoms such as cough or difficulty breathing, assess the duration of symptoms, the presence of paroxysms, whooping, vomiting, or cyanosis, and any history of exposure to TB or HIV infection. Evaluate vaccination history and family history of asthma. 10. On physical examination, look for signs such as lower chest wall indrawing, hyperinflated chest, displaced apex beat, tracheal deviation, raised jugular venous pressure, coarse crackles, bronchial breath sounds, wheezing, or percussion findings indicative of pleural effusion or pneumothorax. 11. Use pulse oximetry to detect hypoxia and guide oxygen therapy. Perform a chest X-ray in cases of severe pneumonia, non-responsive pneumonia, or unclear diagnosis. 12. Pneumonia is classified as severe or non-severe based on clinical features. Severe pneumonia requires hospitalization, oxygen therapy if oxygen saturation is below 90%, and administration of recommended antibiotics such as IV ampicillin and gentamicin. 13. For non-severe pneumonia, provide home care with oral antibiotics like amoxicillin, and advise caregivers on when to return for follow-up or seek immediate medical attention. 14. Avoid unnecessary medications such as those containing atropine, codeine derivatives, or alcohol. 15. For children with severe pneumonia, monitor for improvement within two days, including slower breathing, reduced chest indrawing, less fever, improved feeding, and better oxygen saturation. 16. If complications such as pleural effusion or empyema are suspected, perform a chest X-ray and consider drainage if necessary. Persistent fever despite antibiotic therapy and cloudy or purulent pleural fluid are indicative of empyema. 17. Address risk factors for respiratory illnesses, such as malnutrition, indoor air pollution, and parental smoking, during follow-up care. 18. For children with persistent cough and fever lasting more than two weeks, evaluate for tuberculosis, especially in malnourished children or those with known HIV exposure or infection. 19. Ensure continuous oxygen supply for children with hypoxia, using nasal prongs as the preferred method of oxygen delivery. Monitor oxygen saturation and discontinue oxygen therapy once stable levels are achieved. 20. Discharge criteria for children with severe pneumonia include resolution of respiratory distress, absence of hypoxemia, adequate feeding, and completion of parenteral antibiotic therapy. Arrange follow-up to monitor nutrition and address risk factors.
